Reviewed sources and the chapter contract

This chapter teaches array representation, safe indexing and exact array transformations from first principles. It assumes that you can trace assignments, loops and function calls. The main language is C17. Explicitly marked comparisons use C0, Python 3 or C++. Mathematical algorithms use unbounded integers unless a machine range is specified. Numerical memory diagrams use a stated flat byte-address model; they do not authorize otherwise invalid C pointer operations.

Four primary written courses contribute different parts of the explanation: Cambridge Programming in C (Neel Krishnaswami, 2017–18), CMU 15-122 (Frank Pfenning and André Platzer, Fall 2026), Harvard CS50x (David J. Malan, 2025), and UC Berkeley CS61A / Composing Programs (John DeNero). Stanford CS106B (Chris Gregg, Fall 2016) is a fifth reviewed comparison for dynamic backing arrays. MIT 6.0001 (Ana Bell, Eric Grimson and John Guttag, Fall 2016) is a sixth reviewed comparison for list cloning and mutation during iteration. The source review records exact reading ranges, evaluated alternatives, selection criteria and corrections. References at the end link to written materials.

The central skill is to distinguish four things: a logical sequence, its allocated storage, the references that select that storage, and the sequence of writes that changes it. Address arithmetic alone cannot establish correctness. Every problem needs a domain, an access proof, a value relation and an explanation of whether the relation uses original or already modified values.

After reading, you should be able to derive row/column strides, invert a flat index, classify C array expressions, prove loop and copy invariants, detect alias corruption, calculate dynamic-array costs and explain Python shallow sharing. The worked bank emphasizes these mathematical and conceptual tasks. Two authentic examination items are explicitly labeled bridge revisits rather than newly discovered unique items. No finite source pool or test suite can guarantee all future examination questions.

Elements, boundaries and object representation

An abstract array of length n maps each integer index in 0≤i<n to one element. An array can repeat values; positions remain distinct even when values are equal. A segment A[l:r) contains indices l,l+1,…,r-1, requires 0≤l≤r≤n, and has length r-l. Its right boundary is not an element. The empty segment A[k:k) is valid for every boundary 0≤k≤n.

For a language with lower bound L and upper bound U, the length is U-L+1. The normalized index is i-L. A zero-length abstract sequence is useful, but a standard fixed C declaration cannot use a zero array bound. An empty logical sequence may instead have reserved capacity, or be represented by a pointer and length zero. A variable-length C array evaluated with a nonpositive bound is also invalid; do not turn a mathematical empty case into such a declaration.

A C array is a contiguous object consisting of elements of one element type. There is no extra gap between successive elements beyond what is included in each element's own size. An array of structures therefore uses the structure's full size, including any structure padding, as its stride. A pointer object stores a pointer value; it does not contain the whole pointed-to array. A Python list is a mutable sequence of object references and can contain heterogeneous objects. Its language contract does not promise the same raw layout as a C integer array.

Write the following initialization before doing any arithmetic:

int a[6] = {4, -2, 7};   /* Remaining elements are zero. */
int b[6];               /* Automatic elements are not initialized here. */
static int c[6];         /* Static-storage elements are zero-initialized. */

The first array has six elements, not three; the initializer leaves the final three equal to zero. Reading an uninitialized automatic integer element does not give a portable predictable value. An arbitrary external input array also needs an explicit validity and initialization assumption.

If the first element begins at byte address B and each element occupies w bytes, then the numerical storage model gives

addr(A[i])=B+w(i-L).

For A[-2:5] with inclusive declaration bounds, B=1200 and w=4, element 3 is at 1200+4(3+2)=1220. This example uses a language-independent declaration; ordinary C indices still start at zero. The array's final occupied byte is B+wn-1, while its one-past boundary is B+wn. Neither an arbitrary byte address nor a numerically aligned address proves that a live typed C object exists there.

Multidimensional layouts and inverse indices

A rectangular two-dimensional array with R rows and C columns has RC elements. Let row and column lower bounds be Lr,Lc, and normalize u=i-Lr, v=j-Lc. In row-major storage, all C entries of each earlier row precede the selected row, then v entries precede the selected column. Consequently,

orow=uC+v,addr(A[i,j])=B+w(uC+v).

In column-major storage, each earlier column contains R entries:

ocol=vR+u,addr(A[i,j])=B+w(vR+u).

These expressions count elements first and bytes second. For

R=3,C=4,w=8,B=2048

, index (2,1) has row-major offset 9 and address 2120; its column-major offset is 5 and address 2088. C's real rectangular array declaration uses row-major storage. Column-major here is a separate stated representation, not a switch in how C interprets its declared array.

The inverse follows from quotient and remainder. Given a valid row-major element offset 0≤o<RC, divide o by C: u=⌊o/C⌋ and v=omodC. For column-major, divide by R to recover v and u. For a byte address X, first check that X-B is nonnegative, divisible by w, and less than wRC. A byte inside an element is not necessarily that element's starting address.

For three normalized indices u,v,t in extents D1,D2,D3, row-major offset is

o=(uD2+v)D3+t=uD2D3+vD3+t.

This is mixed-radix notation. Its uniqueness follows by repeatedly taking remainder and quotient by the last extent. In d dimensions, the stride of axis k in row-major order is the product of all later extents. Changing one index by one changes the element offset by that stride. The same principle handles a general affine view with stated strides sk: o=∑k(ik-Lk)sk. Such a view may include gaps or reversed axes; it need not be a standalone C multidimensional array.

A true C declaration and an array of row pointers are different:

int grid[3][4];
int (*row)[4] = grid;  /* Pointer to a complete four-int row. */
int *rows[3];         /* Array of three int pointers: pointees need allocation. */

The first contains twelve integer objects. Its expression conversion gives a pointer to a row, so row + 1 advances by four integers. The last contains three pointer objects and makes no promise that the selected row allocations are adjacent, equally long or even valid. Casting grid to int ** cannot create the missing row-pointer objects. A numerical flattening formula also does not justify using pointer arithmetic beyond the first actual row subarray; for portable C, index grid[i][j] with valid row and column bounds.

Transposition of an R×C row-major logical matrix produces a C×R result. Original position (i,j) maps from iC+j to jR+i. A transpose view can swap strides without moving data; a copied transpose creates a different physical arrangement. Square in-place transposition swaps each pair i<j once and leaves the diagonal unchanged. Rectangular in-place transposition requires permutation cycles or extra storage and cannot use the square-only loop unchanged.

C arrays, pointers and legal accesses

In most expression contexts, a C array expression converts to a pointer to its first element. Important exceptions include an array operand of sizeof, an operand of unary &, and a string literal used to initialize an array. A real array's sizeof counts its full storage. A function parameter declared int a[] is adjusted to int *a, so sizeof a inside that function counts the pointer object. The function must receive an independent length or a stronger explicit contract.

int a[5] = {2, 4, 6, 8, 10};
int *p = a + 2;
int x = p[-1];           /* Selects a[1], so x is 4. */
size_t n = sizeof a / sizeof a[0];  /* Five, in this actual-array scope. */

The subscript p[-1] does not mean “count from the end” as in Python. The identity p[k]=*(p+k) applies only when the resulting access is legal. Here p points at a[2], so -1 moves back to a[1]. For a pointer at a[r], permitted element-access offsets satisfy -r≤k<n-r. Pointer formation additionally permits k=n-r, the one-past position; dereferencing that position does not.

Pointer addition and subtraction must stay within one array object or its one-past boundary. Subtraction counts elements, not bytes, and its result must be representable in ptrdiff_t. The valid numerical byte difference is therefore not a justification for subtracting pointers into unrelated allocations. Relational comparisons between unrelated array pointers likewise cannot be used as a portable general address ordering.

Unary & applied to the complete array yields a pointer to the whole array type. a and &a can describe the same beginning of storage, but their types and increments differ: a + 1 advances one int after conversion; &a + 1 advances one five-int array. Equality of beginning locations is not equality of type or stride.

For an array with nonzero length, a + n is a legal one-past pointer useful as an exclusive end. A reverse loop using size_t must not rely on i >= 0 to stop, because size_t is unsigned. Use a boundary that decreases before the access:

for (size_t i = n; i > 0; ) {
    --i;
    use(a[i]);
}

The body runs n times and never computes n - 1 when n is zero. Check arithmetic used in allocation: before requesting n * sizeof *p bytes, establish

n≤⌊SIZE_MAX/sizeof(*p)⌋

. A successful arithmetic check still needs successful allocation and a live valid object. A successful realloc may move storage and invalidate earlier aliases. For a positive requested size, allocation failure leaves the old allocation valid, so retain its pointer until the result is known. Handle zero-size requests separately under the C17 contract; a null result does not by itself establish a failed positive-size request.

For a rectangular parameter, int a[][4] adjusts to int (*a)[4]. The column extent participates in the row stride. C variable-length parameter forms can express a run-time column count, with the relevant positive-bound and implementation-support conditions; int ** remains a different representation.

Traversals, reductions and proof obligations

Before tracing a loop, describe the exact visited indices. For increasing stride s>0 over the half-open segment [l,r), they are l+ts for nonnegative integers t with l+ts<r. The count is zero when l≥r; otherwise it is ⌈(r-l)/s⌉. For a reverse traversal starting at r-1 with decrement s, the count is the same. A separate stopping relation involving the destination index can prematurely terminate a copying procedure.

To sum a segment, define original values A0[k] and use the invariant

l≤i≤r,S=∑k=li-1A0[k].

Initially i=l and the empty sum is zero. The guard i<r together with the invariant proves a valid read. Adding the current value and advancing i extends the sum by exactly one term. At exit, i=r, so the required segment sum is obtained. The variant r-i decreases to zero. Machine integer addition separately needs representability of all partial sums.

Finding a minimum needs a nonempty input or an explicit optional-result convention. If the first element initializes the minimum, comparisons number n-1. If a mathematical positive-infinity sentinel initializes it, comparisons number n and the first value always causes an update. Strict comparison retains the first occurrence of a tied minimum; non-strict comparison retains the last. Do not assume independence when analyzing the random number of updates; the authentic PhD bridge below derives it with indicator expectations.

For prefix sums, reserve n+1 entries and define

P[0]=0,P[i+1]=P[i]+A[i],∑k=lr-1A[k]=P[r]-P[l].

The query formula follows by cancellation of the first l terms, and also works for an empty segment. A static array permits linear preprocessing and constant-time range-sum queries. A later element update invalidates every subsequent prefix value; do not claim unchanged query correctness after mutation.

For positive length n, an n-entry difference sequence satisfies D[0]=A[0] and D[i]=A[i]-A[i-1] for 0<i<n. For n equal to zero, the sequence is empty and neither index zero is read. A valid update on A[l:r) with l equal to r is a no-op, including the boundary case l = r = n. Otherwise 0≤l<r≤n proves that D[l] exists: add c there, and subtract c from D[r] only when r < n. These boundary changes reconstruct the intended range update by prefix accumulation. An explicitly allocated n+1 boundary representation can instead retain a right-end sentinel, but it is a different storage contract; an n-entry D has no element D[n].

For a two-dimensional prefix table indexed by boundaries, P has shape (R+1)×(C+1) and zero top/left edges. The recurrence and rectangle query are

P[i+1,j+1]=A[i,j]+P[i,j+1]+P[i+1,j]-P[i,j],
S=P[r2,c2]-P[r1,c2]-P[r2,c1]+P[r1,c1].

The final plus sign restores the overlap that the two subtractions removed twice. Half-open row and column bounds make empty rectangles and edge rectangles work without case-specific index subtraction. Native formulas below use a separate mathematical font.

Mutation order, copying and overlap

An in-place transformation reads the values currently stored, unless it explicitly snapshots the original input. For a=[1,2,3,4], the forward update a[i] += a[i-1] for i=1..3 produces [1,3,6,10], because each read uses a modified predecessor. Running the same statements in reverse produces [1,3,5,7], because the predecessor has not yet changed. Both are well-defined mathematical sequences of statements; they compute different maps.

For a copy between distinct arrays, let B receive A[l:r). After t iterations, the copy invariant states B[k]=A0[l+k] for 0≤k<t and 0≤t≤r-l. Destination index t and source index l+t are valid under the segment contract. The result array must have capacity at least r-l; a new allocation gives a distinct result even when the values match.

For a move within the same array from [s,s+m) to [d,d+m), original values are the desired specification. If d > s and the segments overlap, increasing-index copying overwrites source values that have not yet been read. Copy from the high end. If d < s, increasing-index copying is safe; decreasing-index copying may corrupt the source. If d=s, no change is required.

A rigorous reverse-copy invariant fixes the already copied suffix to original values and states that the remaining source prefix is unmodified. At step t descending from m-1, destination d+t lies above source s+t, so it cannot overwrite any still unread smaller source index. This is the reason for the direction, not a convention to memorize.

For disjoint arrays, source and destination are different objects. For a C move within one known backing array, compare integer offsets to select the direction. Do not compare unrelated pointers with > as a general portable overlap test. The library memmove supports valid overlapping byte regions using an as-if temporary-copy contract. memcpy requires nonoverlap. A language-level element-copy loop is more appropriate for object types whose semantics are not simply raw byte copying.

The reviewed CMU copying proof omits an important alias restriction: its postcondition compares final source and final target segments. When overlapping writes modify the source, even the asserted copied-prefix relation can fail. This chapter uses original-input snapshots in its specification and either disjointness or an overlap-safe move. The correction is demonstrated in both the problem bank and an animation.

A complete overlap-safe element implementation

The following function moves elements within one known integer array. Its caller supplies a live initialized backing array with n elements whenever a nonempty move is requested. The function validates offsets before subtraction, so its tests do not themselves overflow. A zero-length move performs no pointer arithmetic or access and may use a null backing pointer. No unrelated-pointer ordering is needed.

#include <stdbool.h>
#include <stddef.h>

bool move_ints(int *a, size_t n, size_t s, size_t d, size_t m) {
    if (s > n || d > n) return false;
    if (m > n - s || m > n - d) return false;
    if (m == 0 || s == d) return true;
    if (d > s) {
        size_t k = m;
        while (k > 0) {
            --k;
            a[d + k] = a[s + k];
        }
    } else {
        for (size_t k = 0; k < m; ++k)
            a[d + k] = a[s + k];
    }
    return true;
}

For the descending branch, at boundary k the target suffix with relative indices k through m−1 equals the corresponding original source suffix. The original source prefix with relative indices below k remains unchanged. After decrement, the read occurs at s+k and the write at d+k. Since d>s, the write is strictly above that source position and therefore above every remaining unread source position. The access checks give s+k<n and d+k<n without requiring an unchecked sum s+m. At k=0, the target is the entire original segment. The ascending branch has the dual invariant: the completed target prefix is correct, and the unread source suffix remains original because d<s. Both branches decrease their number of unprocessed elements by one. For a disjoint rightward move, descending order remains correct even though forward order would also work.

These validations establish ranges, not allocation authenticity: a caller that lies about n or supplies an expired pointer violates the backing-object contract. Returning true means the stated move was performed under that contract; it cannot prove facts about memory that C does not expose as metadata.

To insert at index k in a logical sequence of length n with spare capacity, move original positions n-1 down to k into positions n down to k+1, then write the new element and increase the length. There are n-k shifts. Deletion at k uses forward moves from k+1 through n-1 and decreases the length, for n-k-1 shifts. Old bytes outside the shortened logical prefix need not vanish; capacity and logical length are different.

Reversal swaps (l+t,r-1-t) for 0≤t<⌊(r-l)/2⌋. Its invariant fixes both completed ends and preserves the original untouched middle. Three reversals rotate a nonempty sequence left by k: reverse [0:k), reverse [k:n), then reverse [0:n). Normalizing k modulo n requires n>0; handle the empty sequence before that division. A cycle method uses gcd(n,k) cycles and visits every index exactly once.

The boundary form below avoids unsigned n−1 when the segment is empty. The caller validates l≤r≤n and the backing array before entry. In each iteration r−l>1 guarantees two distinct live indices after decrementing r. An odd middle entry is left alone; there are exactly floor((r−l)/2) pair swaps relative to the original segment length.

void reverse_segment(int *a, size_t l, size_t r) {
    while (r - l > 1) {
        --r;
        int saved = a[l];
        a[l] = a[r];
        a[r] = saved;
        ++l;
    }
}

Why a range check can itself be unsafe

A specification is executable arithmetic, so its precondition must not assume the very safety it is meant to prove. Suppose a nonnegative index type wraps modulo 256, an array has length 20, the proposed start is 250, and the count is 10. Testing start+count<=20 after the wrapped addition accepts 4<=20, even though the first element is already outside the array. In a language whose signed overflow is undefined, evaluating the overflowing sum can instead invalidate the check itself. Neither behavior establishes a valid range.

First check start<=length and then count<=length-start. Short-circuit evaluation must perform the first check before the subtraction. For signed inputs, reject negative start, length and count as well, before converting to an unsigned index type. For the example, 250<=20 immediately fails. For start=20 and count=0, both tests succeed: the empty range ends at a boundary and performs no element access. For start=20 and count=1, the second test fails. Apply this contract separately to source and destination. This strengthens the CMU copying specification without importing C0's arithmetic and allocation assumptions into C17.

Arithmetic validity is only one layer. The claimed length must describe a live backing object; initialization must cover every read; and overlapping writes must preserve every value that is still needed. A successful range check does not establish any of those independent facts. Use an original-input snapshot to state the postcondition when the final source may have been mutated by overlapping destination writes.

A complete method for a new array question

Begin by naming the model: mathematical indexing, C17, Python 3, or an explicitly stipulated byte layout. Record index origins, dimensions, element width, logical length and allocated capacity. If they are absent, state the missing assumption rather than inventing a numerical address or an execution result. In C, the relevant boundary belongs to the pointed-to array object, including a row subarray; numeric adjacency to another row does not enlarge it.

Next express the exact operation before counting it. For a left rotation, new[i]=old[(i+k) mod n], whereas a value originally at i moves to (i-k) mod n. For a half-open slice, the stop is excluded. For an in-place loop, write down the first two actual reads and writes: they expose whether the next read consumes an original value or an overwritten value. For shared Python lists, draw object identities and references before computing printed contents; equal values alone cannot reveal sharing.

Then derive an invariant, prove its initial case, show preservation for one operation and identify the decreasing measure. Count the quantity the question actually requests: comparisons, assignments, copies, calls, occupied bytes or peak simultaneously live storage. These counts can differ even when the algorithm has one asymptotic complexity. Finally test the empty and singleton cases, the first and last valid indices, ties, overlap in both directions and the first arithmetic value beyond the allowed range. A small trace is an independent check of a derivation; it does not replace the general proof.

Python slices, sharing and nested rows

Python single indexing normalizes a negative integer i to n+i and then requires a valid element. Slicing instead normalizes and clips boundaries, then follows a nonzero step. Positive steps default to start zero and stop n; negative steps default to start n-1 and a special before-first stop. The special omitted stop is different from an explicit -1, which normalizes to the last index. Consequently a[::-1] reverses a sequence, while a[:-1:-1] is empty.

After normalization, positive-step selected indices are a+ts<b and negative-step selected indices are a+ts>b. Counting them gives a ceiling divided by the step magnitude when the respective interval is nonempty. Use slice(...).indices(n) when auditing Python's exact boundary normalization. A zero step raises ValueError; an out-of-range single index raises IndexError, while a clipped ordinary slice can simply be empty.

a = [[2], [5]]
b = a[:]             # New outer list, same inner lists.
b[0].append(7)       # Also visible through a[0].
b[1] = [9]           # Rebinds only b's second slot.

After the first mutation, both outer lists contain a first reference to [2,7]. After the second, a is [[2,7],[5]] and b is [[2,7],[9]]. A shallow copy does not copy recursively referenced objects. A row comprehension that creates a fresh row each time avoids the repeated-row problem:

bad = [[0] * 3] * 2
good = [[0] * 3 for _ in range(2)]
bad[0][1] = 8         # Both displayed rows change.
good[0][1] = 8        # Only the first row changes.

An ordinary step-one slice assignment can change the list's length. An extended slice with a step other than one requires exactly as many replacement items as selected slots. Mutating a list while iterating can skip shifted elements: the iterator advances its position while deletion moves the next element left. A safe filtering construction makes a new output or uses a carefully proved read/write compaction loop.

Python string elements are Unicode code points, whereas C char-array bytes and UTF-8 encoding lengths describe different units. One displayed grapheme may contain several code points. Reversal by code points is not automatically a correct visual reversal of human text. These distinctions prevent importing a byte-address formula into Python string indexing.

C strings, terminators and bounded searching

A C string is a sequence of character values ending at its first zero character within accessible storage. Capacity, initialized bytes and string length are separate quantities. char s[] = "cat" allocates four characters; strlen(s) is three and sizeof s is four in that actual-array scope. char t[3] = "cat" is allowed in C but lacks the terminator, so it is not a valid string for strlen or %s. An embedded zero ends the string earlier even if later bytes remain in the array.

The string literal used through const char *p = "cat" must not be modified. A writable array initialized from the literal can be modified within its bounds. p's sizeof measures the pointer. strlen requires a terminator and scans up to it; the return type is size_t, not int. The final zero is a real array element, unlike the one-past pointer.

Searching m pattern characters in a text of length n requires candidate starts 0≤s≤n-m when m≤n. Each comparison reads text[s+t] with 0≤t<m, hence s+t<n. In the worst case, a direct search performs (n-m+1)m character comparisons, but successful early matches and mismatches can reduce that count. For m=0, specify a match at the starting boundary. For m>n, return failure before subtracting unsigned lengths.

def first_match(text, pattern):
    n, m = len(text), len(pattern)
    if m == 0:
        return 0
    if m > n:
        return -1
    for start in range(n - m + 1):
        j = 0
        while j < m and text[start + j] == pattern[j]:
            j += 1
        if j == m:
            return start
    return -1

This code is a complete bounded-search model, not a C library replacement. Returning a C pointer into a caller-owned text additionally depends on that text's lifetime. Command-line argv is an array of pointers to strings, with argv[argc] null; that final pointer is different from each argument's final zero character. If argc is zero, argv[0] is the null sentinel and cannot be read as a program-name string.

Character conversion using a numeric difference assumes an encoding such as ASCII. C's ctype operations accept EOF or an unsigned-char-representable value; a negative signed char must first be converted to unsigned char. Do not assume that bytewise uppercase conversion handles arbitrary UTF-8 text.

Capacity growth and exact operation costs

A dynamic array maintains 0≤n≤c, where n is logical length and c is allocated capacity. Its occupied logical prefix is [0:n); allocated spare slots are [n:c). Insertion requires free capacity or expansion. Expansion allocates a new backing block, copies the n live elements, changes the owning reference and releases the old block under the appropriate ownership rules. Any earlier interior pointer into released storage becomes invalid.

Under the simple doubling model with initial capacity 1, successful appends allocate capacities 1,2,4,8,... . Copy work through a final capacity c is

1+2+4+…+c2=c-1.

For n≥1, the smallest power-of-two c at least n satisfies n≤c<2n. Hence copied elements are less than 2n and total writes including the n new elements are less than 3n. This proves amortized constant append cost under unit-cost element copying, while one expansion append still has linear cost. It does not say that every individual append is constant-time.

Doubling is not uniquely optimal. A fixed factor g>1 also produces a geometric total; its time/space constants differ. An additive increment instead creates quadratic total copying when it is fixed as n grows. Allocation time, element-copy behavior, cache effects and peak memory are outside the simplest unit-copy model and must be stated if included.

When c live elements expand to 2c, both blocks can coexist during copying, so the peak backing capacity is 3c slots. The final capacity alone misses that peak. A container with owned nested allocations also requires correct copy/move semantics; copying pointer values alone may produce shared ownership bugs. Shrinking at exactly half-full can repeatedly grow/shrink under alternating operations. A separate lower shrink threshold supplies hysteresis.

Two-dimensional traversal order affects a stated locality model. For a row-major matrix, visiting successive columns in one row accesses adjacent elements. Visiting one column down the rows uses a stride of C elements. Arithmetic operation counts may be equal while cache-line accesses differ. A precise cache question must state line size, alignment, cache capacity, replacement assumptions and reuse; “row-major is always faster” is not a theorem.

Packed representations and advanced index reasoning

For a lower-triangular n×n matrix storing its diagonal in row order, valid normalized indices satisfy 0≤j≤i<n. Earlier row lengths are 1 through i, so

o=i(i+1)2+j,N=n(n+1)2.

For an upper triangle in row order, row i has n-i entries and earlier rows contain in-i(i-1)/2 entries:

o=in-i(i-1)2+(j-i),0≤i≤j<n.

These are representation-dependent formulas. For a symmetric matrix stored only in its lower triangle, replace (i,j) by

(max(i,j),min(i,j))

before applying the lower formula. Multiplication and division must be ordered or widened so that a finite implementation does not overflow its intermediate product. The final representability of a triangular count does not alone ensure that i(i+1) fits.

A jagged matrix with row lengths r0,…,rR-1 can be packed into one flat sequence using boundary offsets Q[0]=0 and Q[i+1]=Q[i]+ri. Element (i,j) lies at Q[i]+j for 0≤j<ri. Repeated offsets represent empty rows. Recovering a row from a flat position must locate a nonempty interval containing it, rather than taking the first equal boundary blindly.

A circular buffer with positive capacity c maps logical offset t from head h to (h+t)modc. Maintain the length separately to distinguish empty from full when head equals tail. For negative integer rotations, normalize with mathematical modulo in [0:c); C's signed remainder may be negative and requires an explicit correction. The empty-capacity case cannot use modulo at all.

An in-place read/write compaction has invariant 0≤w≤r≤n, with A[0:w) equal to the retained original values from A[0:r) in their original order. Because w never exceeds r, writing A[w] cannot damage unread positions above r. This gives a stable filter with linear reads and at most n writes. It is a proof about dependency direction, closely related to safe leftward copying.

Worked mathematical and conceptual problems

The first two items revisit original MSc/PhD scans. The remaining items are original examination-style questions or independently worded course-inspired extensions, with their origin stated. Solutions explain the model, derive the result and examine a relevant boundary or distractor. Some tasks ask for a proof or behavior classification because a numeric answer would conceal the main issue.

Authentic array-reasoning bridge revisits

Question 1. Recursive reverse-stride copying

Authentic bridge revisit · checked English adaptation

MS CS 1393 · Q167 · PDF page 34. Explicit bridge revisit; independently derived, not an official key.

Copy every other element of an N -element array a, starting at its last element, into array b from index zero upward. Call store(N-1,0). Which pseudocode is correct? Syntax below treats parameters as integers and arrays as available in the procedure.

1.

if(n<0)return; b[i]=a[n]; store(n-2,i+1);

2.

if(n<0)return; b[i+1]=a[n]; store(n-2,i+1);

3.

if(n<0)return; b[i]=a[n]; store(n-2,i+2);

4.

if(n<0)return; b[i+1]=a[n]; store(n-2,i+2);

Read the complete derivation and reasoning

Correct option: 1.

Let t count completed copies. At the beginning of a call, the required indices are n=N-1-2t and i=t, while each already written destination b[j] equals original source a[N-1-2j] for 0≤j<t. The initial call establishes this relation with an empty prefix. A nonnegative n permits exactly the next desired copy; decreasing n by two and increasing i by one preserves the invariant. The negative guard occurs before any invalid read.

For N=6 and a=[10,20,30,40,50,60], source indices 5,3,1 write [60,40,20] at consecutive destinations 0,1,2. The terminal call receives n=-1. For odd N=5, the selected indices are 4,2,0 and the terminal n is -2, so changing the guard to n<=0 would wrongly omit index zero. The general write count is ⌈N/2⌉, with one additional guard-only invocation. No writes occur on unwinding.

All four original alternatives use the correct source stride minus two and the guard n<0. Option 2 starts at destination one; option 3 writes at zero,two,four,...; option 4 combines destination origin one and stride two. Only option 1 gives the required contiguous output. The independently derived answer is one, not a verified official key.

This is legacy integer pseudocode with globally available arrays. A real implementation needs a sufficiently large destination, valid indices and preservation of unread source values through separate storage or a proved overlap strategy. The mathematical empty extension copies nothing and makes one guard call, but is not an assertion that the original exam explicitly stipulated an empty input. This placement is an identified bridge revisit.

Exact-input visual solution

Each write uses a source index decreasing by two and a contiguous destination index.

Copy source index 5 into destination 0.

Question 2. Expected running-minimum updates

Authentic bridge revisit · checked English adaptation

Phd CS 1404 · Q72 · PDF page 16. Explicit bridge revisit; independently derived, not an official key.

A contains n distinct finite values, with every permutation equally likely. The original mathematical pseudocode is:

min = +infinity
for (i = 1; i <= n; i++)
    if (min > A[i])
        min = A[i]  // counted assignment

Y counts executions of the marked assignment. Which listed expression approximates its mean asymptotically? The original asks which expression is closer to the mean; this English adaptation makes its intended large-n comparison explicit.

1.

1

2.
lnn
3.

n

4.
nlnn
Read the complete derivation and reasoning

Correct option: 2.

Define Ii=1 when position i causes the marked assignment, and zero otherwise. This occurs exactly when that position contains the smallest of the first i distinct values. Under the stated uniform permutation model, each of those i positions is equally likely to contain that smallest value, giving P(Ii=1)=1/i.

The counted updates satisfy Y=∑i=1nIi. Linearity of expectation, without requiring independence, therefore gives

E[Y]=∑i=1n1i=Hn.

The exact expectation is a harmonic number. Integration of the decreasing function 1/x yields ln(n+1)≤Hn≤1+lnn, so option 2, ln n, is the intended asymptotic approximation. It is not an identity H_n=ln n and is not necessarily the numerically closest formula for every small n.

For n=3, all six permutations have eleven counted updates in total, giving exact mean 11/6. In the concrete order [5,2,4,1,3], the updates store five, two and one, so Y is three. The scan always makes n element comparisons, but its number of successful assignments varies from one in increasing order to n in decreasing order.

The infinity initialization ensures the first finite value is counted. Initializing instead from the first data element and scanning only the rest removes that update and changes the mean to H_n-1. Duplicates or a nonuniform permutation model require another probability proof. Option 1 misses the growing record count; option n treats every value as a new record; n ln n multiplies rather than sums the per-position probabilities. Both original loop endpoints and strict comparison were inspected on the scan; no official answer key is claimed.

Exact-input visual solution

The source counts successful strict updates after infinity initialization, not every comparison.

Read position 1: strict update.

Original and course-inspired mathematical/conceptual problems

Question 3. A lower bound is not the first value

Original/course-inspired problem · author-assessed medium to hard

Original examination-style problem

A flat representation declares indices -3 through 8 inclusive, four-byte elements and base address 1600 for the first element. Find the address of index 5, total storage and final occupied byte.

Read the complete derivation and reasoning

The inclusive logical interval from minus three through eight contains 8-(-3)+1=12 elements. The first element is at logical index minus three, so the normalized offset of index five is 5-(-3)=8. This counts eight complete element widths before the requested element; it does not use the element's stored value.

With base address 1600 and width four, the requested starting address is

1600+4·8=1632.

All twelve elements occupy 12·4=48 bytes. Consequently the inclusive final occupied byte is 1600+48-1=1647, whereas the one-past boundary is 1648. The last element itself begins at 1600+4·11=1644 and occupies bytes 1644 through 1647. These three endpoints must not be conflated.

As a consistency check, logical index minus three maps to 1600, and index eight maps to 1644. Increasing a valid index by one increases its starting address by exactly four. Computing 1600 plus four times five would incorrectly assume a zero lower bound. This is a numerical flat-storage model with language-independent declaration bounds, not an ordinary C declaration allowing negative array bounds or a claim about portable integer-to-pointer conversion.

Exact-input visual solution

Read the exact quantities and the named model; rows are derivation checkpoints, not assumed physical memory.

Count inclusive indices.

Question 4. Invert a two-dimensional row-major address

Original/course-inspired problem · author-assessed medium to hard

Original examination-style problem

A row-major matrix has row indices 2..6 and column indices -1..5. Each element occupies eight bytes; its first element starts at 4096. Which element starts at address 4312?

Read the complete derivation and reasoning

There are five rows, from two through six, and seven columns, from minus one through five. The byte displacement is 4312-4096=216. Because 216 is divisible by the stated element width eight, the requested address can be an element start. Its normalized element offset is 216/8=27.

For row-major storage, divide by the column extent seven:

27=3·7+6.

Thus the normalized coordinates are (3,6), and adding the declared lower bounds gives row 2+3=5 and column -1+6=5. Reconstructing verifies the answer: 4096+8(3·7+6)=4312. Both declared coordinates lie within their respective bounds, and the flat offset is below the total extent 5·7=35.

If the same declared matrix instead used column-major storage, dividing 27 by five would yield normalized column five and row two, hence logical coordinate (4,4). This distinct valid result explains why stating the layout is necessary. Address 4313 lies inside an element rather than at its start and fails the alignment test before coordinate recovery is attempted.

Exact-input visual solution

Read the exact quantities and the named model; rows are derivation checkpoints, not assumed physical memory.

Check address alignment.

Question 5. Recover a missing column extent

Original/course-inspired problem · author-assessed medium to hard

Original examination-style problem

In row-major storage of four-byte elements, A[1,2] starts at 1028 and A[3,1] starts at 1064. Both dimensions start at zero. Determine the number of columns, then the base address.

Read the complete derivation and reasoning

Let C denote the unknown positive column count and B the starting byte address. With zero-based row-major indices and four-byte elements, the two observations give

1028=B+4(C+2),1064=B+4(3C+1).

Subtracting the equations removes B:

36=4(2C-1).

Therefore 2C-1=9, so C is five. Substitution into the first equation gives B=1028-4·7=1000. The second observation independently reconstructs as 1000+4(3·5+1)=1064.

Column indices one and two are legal for a five-column row, and observing row three requires at least four rows. Nothing in either equation states the final row index, so the total number of rows remains undetermined. Every row count at least four is consistent with these observations under the declared flat layout.

This is an inverse problem with a consistency condition, rather than permission to report any algebraic result as a shape. A noninteger or nonpositive solution for C, or a column observation outside the recovered extent, would invalidate the proposed representation. Once C is known, its byte row stride is twenty; the observed displacement thirty-six equals two row strides minus one element width, exactly matching the move from (1,2) to (3,1).

Question 6. Distinguish row-major from column-major numerically

Original/course-inspired problem · author-assessed medium to hard

Original examination-style problem

A 4×6 matrix begins at 800, uses two-byte elements and zero-based indices. Calculate the address of (2,3) in each layout and explain why the addresses need not differ at every index.

Read the complete derivation and reasoning

The row-major offset of (2,3) in four rows and six columns is 2·6+3=15. With base 800 and two-byte elements, its address is 830. In column-major storage, the offset is 3·4+2=14, giving address 828. These calculations use the same coordinate and different declared storage conventions.

For an arbitrary valid coordinate (i,j), equality of the two offsets requires

iC+j=jR+i,i(C-1)=j(R-1).

Here the condition becomes 5i=3j. Since three and five are coprime, integer solutions have i=3t and j=5t. Within 0≤i<4 and 0≤j<6, only t equal to zero or one is possible. Thus the two matching coordinates are (0,0) and (3,5), the common first and final positions. The requested (2,3) is neither of them.

More generally, for both dimensions greater than one, the number of matching coordinates is gcd(R-1,C-1)+1. The one-row or one-column cases need separate treatment because the two orders then coincide throughout. These formulas compare two numerical representations; they do not make column-major traversal a second interpretation of the type and layout of one declared C rectangular array.

Question 7. Three-dimensional mixed-radix recovery

Original/course-inspired problem · author-assessed medium to hard

Original examination-style problem

A zero-based row-major array has extents 3×4×5, base 2000 and four-byte elements. Find the address of (2,1,3), then recover the indices of element offset 47.

Read the complete derivation and reasoning

For zero-based row-major extents three, four and five, advancing the first coordinate skips twenty elements per unit, advancing the second skips five, and advancing the final coordinate skips one. Coordinate (2,1,3) therefore has offset

2·20+1·5+3=48.

Its starting byte address is 2000+4·48=2192. Each coordinate is legal and offset 48 lies below the total extent sixty.

To recover the coordinate of offset 47, take quotient and remainder by the final extent: 47=9·5+2. Hence the last coordinate is two. Decode the remaining quotient using the middle extent: 9=2·4+1. The first two coordinates are therefore two and one, giving (2,1,2). Reconstruction yields (2·4+1)5+2=47.

This is mixed-radix uniqueness: each remainder is in the valid range of its corresponding axis, and the final first-coordinate quotient must be below three. Simply summing indices loses the skipped rows and planes. Offset sixty would fail the total-extent test even though repeated division could still produce a three-number tuple; the inverse algorithm must validate the recovered leading coordinate too.

Question 8. A transpose changes the destination shape

Original/course-inspired problem · author-assessed medium to hard

Original examination-style problem

A 2×5 row-major matrix is copied into a 5×2 transpose. Where does original flat offset 7 move, and where does offset 9 move?

Read the complete derivation and reasoning

The source has two rows and five columns. For a source flat offset o, recover its coordinates with quotient and remainder by five. Then swap the coordinates, and encode them using the destination's two columns, not the source's five.

For offset seven, 7=1·5+2 identifies source (1,2). Its transpose coordinate is (2,1), whose destination offset is 2·2+1=5. For offset nine, 9=1·5+4 gives source (1,4), destination (4,1), and new offset 4·2+1=9.

In general the mapping is

iC+j⟼jR+i.

It is bijective because destination coordinates (j,i) recover the unique source (i,j), with the destination shape C by R. In this two-by-five case the complete source-to-destination offset list is [0,2,4,6,8,1,3,5,7,9], containing each offset zero through nine exactly once.

The fixed final offset nine therefore does not imply an unchanged arrangement. A transpose view that exchanges strides and a physically copied transpose are distinct implementations of the coordinate relation. Likewise, the pairwise square-matrix swap loop cannot be applied unchanged to this rectangular physical arrangement; its permutation contains longer cycles.

Exact-input visual solution

Read the exact quantities and the named model; rows are derivation checkpoints, not assumed physical memory.

Decode with five columns, encode with two.

Question 9. Affine strides with a reversed axis

Original/course-inspired problem · author-assessed medium to hard

Original examination-style problem

A numerical view has row stride 40 bytes and column stride -4 bytes. Its logical (0,0) starts at address 1020, and its shape is 3×6. Find the addresses of (2,5) and (1,0), and the minimum and maximum selected element-start addresses.

Read the complete derivation and reasoning

The stated numerical affine map is

X(i,j)=1020+40i-4j,0≤i<3,0≤j<6.

Thus X(2,5)=1020+80-20=1080, and X(1,0)=1060. The row term is increasing and the column term is decreasing over independent rectangular index bounds. Its minimum is therefore at (0,5), giving 1000, and its maximum is at (2,0), giving 1100.

The three rows select starting addresses 1020,1016,...,1000; then 1060,1056,...,1040; then 1100,1096,...,1080. This explicit list checks both extrema and exposes the gaps between successive selected row ranges. A shape-only dense row-major formula would incorrectly discard the negative column direction and the forty-byte row stride.

The requested extrema concern element starts. The statement does not explicitly declare element byte width, so it does not by itself determine the final occupied byte. If an additional four-byte-width convention is imposed, the last selected element occupies through 1103. That is a conditional conclusion, not an assumption inferred solely from a stride of minus four. A backing allocation and typed-object contract must also cover all accesses; these numerical addresses alone do not prove valid C pointer arithmetic or provenance.

Question 10. Packed lower triangle and symmetric lookup

Original/course-inspired problem · author-assessed medium to hard

Original examination-style problem

A zero-based symmetric 6×6 matrix stores its lower triangle including the diagonal, in row order, with eight-byte elements and base 3000. Find the stored address for logical (1,4).

Read the complete derivation and reasoning

Only lower-triangle positions with 0≤j≤i<6 are physically stored. The logical request (1,4) is above that diagonal. Symmetry of values permits redirecting it to stored coordinate (4,1); without symmetry, this replacement would have no general justification.

Before row four lie rows zero through three, of lengths one, two, three and four. Their total is ten. Column one is one position after the start of stored row four, so its flat offset is eleven and its address is

3000+8·11=3088.

The lower-triangle row-major encoding is i(i+1)/2+j on its declared domain. Substituting (4,1) reproduces eleven. Applying that encoding directly to the unnormalized upper coordinate (1,4) would produce six, but that number denotes a different physical position and is not an alternative correct answer.

The packed representation has 6·7/2=21 stored elements. Its final element starts at 3160, so the requested 3088 lies within the packed extent and has the required eight-byte alignment relative to the base. Equal total storage counts would not identify the order by themselves: storing columns, omitting the diagonal or packing the upper triangle would require a different coordinate formula.

Question 11. Packed upper triangle cannot reuse the lower formula

Original/course-inspired problem · author-assessed medium to hard

Original examination-style problem

An upper-triangular 5×5 matrix includes its diagonal and is packed by rows. Find the flat offset of (2,4), and identify which coordinates occupy flat offset 9.

Read the complete derivation and reasoning

In an upper triangle of order five, stored row lengths are five, four, three, two and one. Before row two there are five plus four, or nine entries. That row begins at column two, so column four is two positions later. Its flat offset is 9+(4-2)=11.

To invert offset nine, locate its row interval. Row zero occupies [0,5), row one [5,9), and row two [9,12). Therefore offset nine is the first entry of row two, coordinate (2,2), rather than the final entry of row one.

For general order n and a valid upper coordinate 0≤i≤j<n, the preceding rows contain

∑r=0i-1(n-r)=in-i(i-1)2.

Adding within-row offset j-i gives the full encoding. This is not the lower-triangle prefix i(i+1)/2, because row lengths decrease instead of increase. Both conventions happen to store n(n+1)/2 entries, but equal capacities do not imply equal coordinate maps.

The half-open row intervals also give a safe inverse strategy: find the unique row whose start is at most the flat offset and whose next start is larger, then add the within-row displacement to that row's diagonal column. A final boundary equal to fifteen is one-past, not a valid stored coordinate.

Question 12. Repeated jagged boundaries

Original/course-inspired problem · author-assessed medium to hard

Original examination-style problem

Rows have lengths [2,0,3,1]. Construct the packed boundary array and recover the logical coordinate for flat offsets 2 and 5.

Read the complete derivation and reasoning

Starting with zero, prefix accumulation of row lengths [2,0,3,1] gives boundary array Q = [0,2,2,5,6]. Row i occupies the half-open flat interval [Q[i],Q[i+1]). Thus row zero contains offsets zero and one; row one contains no offset; row two contains two,three,four; row three contains five.

Offset two therefore belongs to row two at column zero, and offset five belongs to row three at column zero. The duplicate boundary two does not create two copies of an element. It records that the intervening row has length zero.

For a valid flat offset o, the inverse condition is

Q[i]≤o<Q[i+1],j=o-Q[i].

With nondecreasing boundaries and a prior check 0≤o<Q[4], this row can be found as the last boundary not exceeding o, equivalently a right-biased upper-bound search minus one. A first-equal-boundary rule fails at repeated boundaries: it can select the empty row one for offset two.

The input bound check is essential. Offset six is the final one-past boundary, so no row owns it. Repeated trailing boundaries from empty final rows do not change that conclusion. This representation packs element storage contiguously while allowing rows to have different lengths; it is not a dense rectangular matrix with one fixed row stride.

Exact-input visual solution

Read the exact quantities and the named model; rows are derivation checkpoints, not assumed physical memory.

First row has two values.

Question 13. Diagonal offsets and loop count

Original/course-inspired problem · author-assessed medium to hard

Original examination-style problem

For an n×n dense row-major matrix, derive the diagonal offsets and their sum, then evaluate for n=5. Count distinct positions selected.

Read the complete derivation and reasoning

For zero-based diagonal coordinate (i,i) in a dense n-by-n row-major matrix, each earlier row contributes n elements and the column contributes another i. The flat offset is therefore in+i=i(n+1) for 0≤i<n.

There are n selected coordinates. Their offsets form an arithmetic progression with first term zero, last term (n-1)(n+1) and spacing n+1. Hence

∑i=0n-1i(n+1)=(n+1)n(n-1)2.

For n equal to five, the selected offsets are [0,6,12,18,24], and their sum is sixty. The selection contains five positions, not twenty-five; the underlying matrix's capacity is not the number of loop visits on its diagonal.

For a nonempty matrix the offsets are distinct because n+1 is positive. At n equal to one, the only offset is zero. At n equal to zero, the abstract index set is empty, the count and sum are zero, and the symbolic formula agrees. This mathematical convention does not license a standard C fixed-size array with a zero bound. Finally, these are sums of positions: the sum of matrix values on those positions cannot be recovered without data values or a separate rule relating values to offsets.

Question 14. When is a flat byte difference meaningful?

Original/course-inspired problem · author-assessed medium to hard

Original examination-style problem

Two separate malloc allocations appear at numerical addresses 1000 and 1040 on one run. Each stores integers. Is their C pointer difference necessarily ten? Explain what additional facts are needed.

Read the complete derivation and reasoning

The observed numerical difference is forty bytes, but C pointer subtraction requires more than a numerical address representation. Both pointer operands must designate elements of one array object, or its permitted one-past position, and the resulting element difference must be representable in ptrdiff_t. Two separate live allocations do not satisfy that shared-array requirement merely because their addresses happen to be near each other.

Moreover, the stem does not state sizeof(int). If a particular implementation uses four-byte integers, forty divided by four is ten as a numerical calculation. That conditional arithmetic does not make subtraction between the actual unrelated pointers defined. If the width is different, even the numerical quotient changes.

Under a different valid setup, let p designate element zero and q designate element ten of one sufficiently large live integer array, with a representable difference. Then q-p equals ten elements regardless of the byte width. Reversing the subtraction yields minus ten. If q is the permitted one-past element at index ten of a ten-element array, subtraction can still be valid although dereferencing q is not.

This separates three facts: byte-address arithmetic in a stipulated representation, element-distance arithmetic within a known array, and legal element access. Neither alignment nor a plausible integer result can substitute for the missing object-domain condition.

Question 15. Interior negative indexing is ordinary pointer arithmetic

Original/course-inspired problem · author-assessed medium to hard

Original examination-style problem

For int a[7]={2,4,6,8,10,12,14}, let p=a+4. Evaluate p[-3], p[2], and the complete range of legal element-access offsets k.

Read the complete derivation and reasoning

The pointer p designates a[4], whose value is ten. Subscript syntax means pointer displacement followed by access: p[k] selects a[4+k] when that element exists. Consequently p[-3] selects a[1] and reads four, while p[2] selects a[6] and reads fourteen.

Solve the access constraint before interpreting any other displacement:

0≤4+k<7⟺-4≤k≤2.

The lower endpoint selects a[0], and the upper selects a[6]. Pointer formation has a slightly larger range: k equal to three forms a+7, the one-past pointer. That endpoint is useful for a boundary comparison or legal same-array subtraction, but not for an evaluated element access. A displacement below minus four or above three exceeds even the pointer-formation domain.

The negative sign is therefore not inherently an error and does not invoke Python's indexing-from-the-end convention. Its legality follows from p's interior position in this same live initialized array. A pointer with the same numerical address but no established object relation would require a separate argument; numerical arithmetic alone is insufficient.

Question 16. Array sizeof and parameter sizeof

Original/course-inspired problem · author-assessed medium to hard

Original examination-style problem

Assume sizeof(int)=4 and sizeof(int *)=8. For a real int a[9], evaluate sizeof a / sizeof a[0]. What does the same expression mean inside void f(int a[9])?

Read the complete derivation and reasoning

Where a is the actual nine-int array object, its size is 9·4=36 bytes and an element's size is four. The quotient is therefore nine. The array operand of sizeof does not undergo the usual conversion to a pointer.

Inside the parameter declaration void f(int a[9]), the parameter is adjusted to int *a. No nine-element array parameter object is created. Under the stated pointer size, sizeof a is eight and sizeof a[0] is four, giving the quotient two. That two is a ratio of type sizes, not a discovered sequence length.

The two expressions have identical spelling but different operand types. Changing the caller's actual array length does not change the adjusted pointer type or its sizeof. Conversely, changing the implementation's pointer size can change the misleading parameter quotient without changing the caller's nine elements.

These fixed-type sizeof expressions do not read any element value. To process the actual sequence, pass a length and require that it matches accessible initialized storage; merely writing nine inside ordinary array-parameter brackets does not supply the length at runtime.

Question 17. Whole-array pointer versus first-element pointer

Original/course-inspired problem · author-assessed medium to hard

Original examination-style problem

For int a[6] and sizeof(int)=4, compare the numerical advances of a+1 and &a+1. Why can both begin at the same storage?

Read the complete derivation and reasoning

In a+1, ordinary expression conversion first gives a pointer to the first int. Adding one advances to the next int, a numerical displacement of four bytes under this problem's stated model. Its resulting type is int*.

Unary & instead preserves the array object as its operand. The type of &a is a pointer to an array of six ints, written int (*)[6]. Adding one advances by one whole pointed-to array, numerically 6·4=24 bytes. The result is one past that entire object and does not designate a second live six-int array.

Both original pointers correspond to the beginning of the same storage because the first element starts at the array's beginning. A common starting location does not erase the pointed-to type, which determines the arithmetic unit. The byte displacements are statements in the specified representation; C does not generally promise that casting pointers to integers produces a universally linear address encoding.

Formation of the whole-array one-past pointer is permitted. Evaluated access through it is not. Changing the array extent to seven would change the whole-array stride to twenty-eight while leaving the element stride four.

Question 18. A row pointer retains the inner extent

Original/course-inspired problem · author-assessed medium to hard

Original examination-style problem

For int m[3][5] with four-byte integers, let p=m. Interpret p+2, *(p+2), and sizeof *(p+2). Is p correctly declared int **?

Read the complete derivation and reasoning

The compatible declaration is int (*p)[5] = m. Conversion of the outer array gives a pointer to its first five-int row. Each row occupies twenty bytes, so p+2 advances forty bytes and designates m[2].

The expression *(p+2) is that five-element row-array lvalue. In an ordinary value context it can convert to a pointer to m[2][0]; as the operand of sizeof it retains its array type. Therefore sizeof *(p+2) is twenty bytes, not the size of an int pointer.

An int** expects a pointer to an int* object. The rectangular matrix stores rows of integers and has no intervening array of row-pointer objects. A cast does not construct those missing objects, so using an int** interpretation is not a representation repair.

There are three separately valid row positions for p-relative row access: zero, one and two. After selecting a row, a column access must also be in zero through four. The two-dimensional numerical offset formula counts storage correctly only when the actual typed accesses respect those separate row and element domains.

Question 19. Numerical adjacency does not erase a C subarray boundary

Original/course-inspired problem · author-assessed medium to hard

Original examination-style problem

For int m[2][3], does a int *p=m[0] authorize p[4] merely because the matrix stores six adjacent integers?

Read the complete derivation and reasoning

The converted m[0] points into the first three-int row object. Relative element pointers p, p+1 and p+2 designate that row's elements, while p+3 is its one-past pointer. Forming p+4 already exceeds that row's permitted pointer-arithmetic domain. Thus p[4] is not justified by the fact that the enclosing rectangular matrix occupies contiguous storage.

The intended element can instead be selected as m[1][1]. The first subscript selects a valid row of the outer two-row array, and the second selects a valid element of that row. Its flat numerical offset is four, but numerical offset and legal typed evaluation are different propositions.

A genuine flat six-int array would have a different relevant element-array domain and could permit flat[4]. The distinction is not whether a processor could reach the bytes. The C object model sets the arithmetic boundary. The public C draft's Annex J.2 explicitly lists an out-of-range multidimensional index despite apparently accessible adjacent storage, reinforcing this point. No compiler observation of a convenient output would establish portable behavior for the invalid expression.

Question 20. Partial initialization and definite values

Original/course-inspired problem · author-assessed medium to hard

Original examination-style problem

At block scope consider int a[5]={9,2}; int b[5]; static int c[5]; Which values of a[4], b[4], c[4] are determined by these declarations?

Read the complete derivation and reasoning

The aggregate initializer supplies a[0] equal to nine and a[1] equal to two. Omitted elements of this initialized aggregate receive zero initialization, so a[2], a[3] and a[4] are zero. The requested a[4] is therefore zero even though only two values were explicitly written.

The block-scope static array c has static storage duration. With no explicit initializer, its integer elements are zero-initialized, so c[4] is also zero. This is a storage-duration initialization guarantee, not a claim that every block-local array starts cleared.

The ordinary automatic b has no initializer. Its element at index four has an indeterminate value; the declaration does not justify a portable numeric result from reading it. Index four is within the allocated five-element array, so the issue is initialization rather than bounds.

A correct access argument checks three facts: the object is alive, the selected index belongs to it, and the stored value can be used under the language rules. Zeroing b explicitly, initializing it with {0}, or giving it static storage would change the last fact. Changing arbitrary observed bytes or guessing previous stack contents is not a valid substitute.

Question 21. Constraint violation is not a surprise numeric output

Original/course-inspired problem · author-assessed medium to hard

Original examination-style problem

Which declarations or statements require a C diagnostic: int a[3]; int b[3]; a=b; int z[0];? How do you copy the contents instead?

Read the complete derivation and reasoning

The positive-bound declarations int a[3] and int b[3] are valid. The assignment a=b violates a constraint: the assignment's left operand must be a modifiable lvalue, and an array is not one. Usual expression conversion does not turn the original array object into a writable pointer variable.

The constant bound in int z[0] is zero, violating the positive-bound requirement for this standard fixed array declaration. A compiler may diagnose and then accept an extension; that does not change its standard-C classification. This differs from a runtime nonpositive variable-length bound, whose rule must be analyzed separately.

To copy initialized contents, use a bounded element loop:

for (size_t i = 0; i < 3; ++i) a[i] = b[i];

Here the original uninitialized b must first receive valid values before this loop reads them. A suitable nonoverlapping byte copy can copy the representation of appropriate objects, but it is not array assignment syntax. Assigning a separate pointer p=b redirects p and copies no array contents. These are distinct operations with different effects.

Question 22. One-past use and dereference are different questions

Original/course-inspired problem · author-assessed medium to hard

Original examination-style problem

For a four-element initialized array, classify a+4, *(a+4), a+5 and (a+4)-a under C17.

Read the complete derivation and reasoning

For this four-element array, a+4 is the permitted one-past pointer. Its formation does not read array contents. It can serve as an exclusive iteration boundary even though it designates no fifth element.

Evaluating *(a+4) as an element indirection is not a valid access. In contrast, a+5 is already outside the permitted pointer-formation range, so no dereference is needed to expose that arithmetic error. The initialized values of the four existing elements do not repair either violation.

The subtraction (a+4)-a uses the same array and its one-past boundary. It gives four in units of elements, subject to representability in ptrdiff_t. It does not need to read a value at the endpoint. Reversing its operands gives minus four under the same representability condition.

The classification concerns evaluated operations. Unevaluated fixed-type sizeof operands and the special cancellation rules for expressions such as &*p need their own analysis; they should not be used to justify an ordinary out-of-bounds read. Keep pointer formation, same-object distance and element access as three separate checks.

Question 23. Unsigned reverse loop trap

Original/course-inspired problem · author-assessed medium to hard

Original examination-style problem

Explain why for(size_t i=n-1; i>=0; --i) use(a[i]); is incorrect. Give a version that also handles n=0 and prove its first and last accessed indices.

Read the complete derivation and reasoning

Because size_t is unsigned, its stored values are never below zero; i>=0 cannot terminate the proposed loop. At n equal to zero, initialization stores the converted value SIZE_MAX in i. For a nonempty array, reaching zero and decrementing similarly produces the maximum unsigned value instead of a negative stopping sentinel. The following access is not a valid reverse traversal.

Use a boundary and decrement before access:

for (size_t i = n; i > 0; ) {
    --i;
    use(a[i]);
}

At every guard, 0≤i≤n. A true guard establishes i positive, so decrement produces a valid index from zero through n-1. The first accessed index is n-1 when n is nonzero; subsequent iterations decrease it by one. After the final access at zero, the next guard sees zero and exits without another decrement.

The variant is the boundary i itself, which decreases on each executed iteration and cannot pass below zero. When n is zero, the body is skipped, including all array access. This proves both the order and the exact n-access count without treating wraparound as termination.

Question 24. A stride count with nonzero boundaries

Original/course-inspired problem · author-assessed medium to hard

Original examination-style problem

A loop visits indices 3,7,11,... while i<26. List the final index and number of visits; derive the count without simulating every iteration.

Read the complete derivation and reasoning

Write a visited index as i=3+4t, where t is a nonnegative iteration number. The condition i<26 becomes 4t<23, hence t can be zero through five. There are six visits: 3,7,11,15,19,23. The last visited index is twenty-three, and the next candidate twenty-seven fails the guard.

Equivalently, a positive stride s over a nonempty half-open interval [l,r) has ⌈(r-l)/s⌉ visits. Here that is ⌈23/4⌉=6. The strict inequality must be retained when converting from an endpoint to an integer count.

Changing the guard to i<=26 happens not to change this example because twenty-six is absent from the progression. At endpoint twenty-seven, the strict guard still excludes that candidate whereas the non-strict guard includes it. A numerical coincidence is therefore not an equivalence proof.

Finally, a zero-based array serving these accesses needs at least twenty-four elements, not merely six. Six counts visits, while twenty-three is the largest accessed coordinate. In actual machine code, the final increment and any arithmetic used to form indices need their own representability check.

Question 25. Two different reduction initializations

Original/course-inspired problem · author-assessed medium to hard

Original examination-style problem

For [5,5,2,2,7,1,1], compare the number of comparisons and successful minimum updates when initialized from the first element versus mathematical positive infinity, always using strict comparison.

Read the complete derivation and reasoning

Initialize the minimum to the first five and scan the six later positions. The second five ties and does not replace a strict minimum; two at index two replaces five; the next two ties; seven is larger; one at index five replaces two; the final one ties. Thus there are six comparisons and two successful updates, with the first minimum occurrence retained at index five.

With a mathematical positive-infinity initialization, all seven elements are compared. The first five now causes an additional successful replacement. The subsequent strict decreases are the same two and one, giving seven comparisons and three updates. Positive infinity is a stated mathematical sentinel, not an arbitrary finite integer constant assumed above every possible input.

Using non-strict comparison would replace on ties too. For this data it would give five updates after first-element initialization, or six after infinity initialization, and retain the last one at index six. That is a different algorithmic policy.

The original strict algorithm's comparison count follows from its scan boundaries; its update count follows from record-low events in the actual data. Neither count alone identifies the other, and a correct final minimum value does not establish the tie index or number of assignments.

Read the exact quantities and the named model; rows are derivation checkpoints, not assumed physical memory.

Infinity makes the first value an update.

Question 26. Weighted prefix invariant

Original/course-inspired problem · author-assessed medium to hard

Original examination-style problem

For mathematical integers A=[2,-1,4,3], compute S=sum((i+1)A[i]) and give a loop invariant for the weighted scan.

Read the complete derivation and reasoning

The four products are 1·2=2, 2·(-1)=-2, 3·4=12 and 4·3=12. Their sum is twenty-four. The running totals after each access are two, zero, twelve and twenty-four.

At a loop boundary use

0≤i≤4,S=∑k=0i-1(k+1)A[k].

Initially i is zero and S is the empty sum zero. A true guard i<4 proves the next element access valid. Adding (i+1)A[i] appends exactly the missing weighted term, and incrementing i restores the stated prefix relation. At exit i=4, the invariant gives the entire required sum. The variant 4-i proves termination.

Using i instead of i+1 changes the products and gives sixteen here, not twenty-four. The unweighted total is eight, another different reduction. The invariant must describe the implemented weighting, not merely mention a generic sum. The question uses mathematical integers; a C implementation would additionally need every multiplication and every partial addition to fit, not just its final result.

Read the complete derivation and reasoning

Set P[0] to zero and successively add the five data values. This constructs P = [0,3,1,6,7,3]. Entry P[t] is the sum of exactly the first t elements, so five elements require six boundary entries.

The sum on [1,4) is P[4]-P[1]=7-3=4, agreeing with the direct sum minus two plus five plus one. The whole-array sum is P[5]-P[0]=3. The empty query [3,3) subtracts P[3] from itself and gives zero without accessing a data element.

Read the complete derivation and reasoning

Use six boundary slots for five data elements and initialize all slots to zero. Adding four on [1,4) records plus four at boundary one and minus four at boundary four. Subtracting two on [2,5) records minus two at boundary two and plus two at boundary five. Their combined difference array is [0,4,-2,0,-4,2].

The final sentinel two cancels the remaining minus-two contribution beyond the data range. Including that sixth accumulated boundary as a data value would incorrectly invent another element. It exists to express the exclusive endpoint, not to extend the logical array.

The boundary prefix table is

P=[00000136051221].

Directly adding the four selected entries 2,3,5,6 also gives sixteen. This independent check detects an indexing convention mismatch.

Question 35. Bounds alone do not prove a copy contract

Original/course-inspired problem · author-assessed medium to hard

A copy_into loop has valid source/destination bounds but its postcondition compares final source and final destination segments. Explain why those bounds are insufficient if both parameters alias.

Read the complete derivation and reasoning

Use one backing array [1,2,3,4], with source zero, target one and length three. Forward copying produces [1,1,1,1]. For a 12-element sequence rotated left by eight, determine the number and length of permutation cycles, and list the cycle beginning at index zero. Use the destination-to-source map (i+8) modulo twelve; distinguish it from original-to-destination movement.

Read the complete derivation and reasoning

The destination-to-source step map for a left rotation by eight is f(i)=(i+8)mod12. Starting at zero gives the cycle 0,8,4,0. Returning after t steps requires twelve to divide 8t. Dividing by their greatest common divisor four shows that the least positive t is three.

All cycles therefore have length three, and the twelve positions form four disjoint cycles. Representatives zero, one, two and three give cycles (0,8,4), (1,9,5), (2,10,6) and (3,11,7). This accounts for every position exactly once.

The orientation matters during implementation. The new value at destination i comes from old position f(i); following this source map with a saved element implements the left rotation. Mapping an old element to its new destination instead uses subtraction of eight modulo twelve, the inverse cycle orientation.

In general, repeated addition of k modulo positive n gives gcd(n,k) cycles of length n/gcd(n,k). Distinct values are unnecessary because the cycles concern positions. For normalized k equal to zero, every position is a one-element cycle and no movement is needed. Repeating a traversal from an already visited member would duplicate work.

Question 42. A stable read/write filter

Original/course-inspired problem · author-assessed medium to hard

Original examination-style problem

Remove odd entries from [5,2,7,4,6,9,8] in place without changing the order of retained entries. Give final logical contents and explain why writes cannot destroy unread data.

Read the complete derivation and reasoning

Read the original sequence from left to right with write boundary w initially zero. Five is rejected. Two is copied to position zero; seven is rejected; four is copied to position one; six to position two; nine is rejected; eight to position three. The final logical prefix is [2,4,6,8] with length four.

At each boundary, 0≤w≤r≤7, and positions before w are exactly the retained values from the processed original prefix before r, in encounter order. On rejection only r advances. On retention, write at w and advance both boundaries, extending the retained prefix by precisely the next qualifying value.

Because w never exceeds r, a write affects the current or an earlier position, never a larger unread one. The original value needed at r is read before that write. This proves interference safety as well as stability.

Spare positions beyond new length four can retain old or copied values; they are not part of the logical result. If no elements qualify the result is an empty prefix, and if all qualify the values remain in their original order. The predicate and capacity contract, not the physical contents of the spare suffix, determine correctness.

Exact-input visual solution

Compare the initial state and the current state. The caption names the exact write or boundary decision.

The retained prefix is initially empty.

Question 43. Direction of an in-place adjacent-difference transform

Original examination-style problem

For A=[3,5,9,10], compute the adjacent differences A[i]-A[i-1] for i>0 in place while retaining A[0]. Which loop direction gives original differences?

Read the complete derivation and reasoning

Process indices three, two and one. The first subtraction is ten minus nine, storing one at index three. Then nine minus five stores four at index two, and five minus three stores two at index one. The result is [3,2,4,1].

At a descending checkpoint, completed suffix positions hold original adjacent differences and the remaining prefix is unchanged. The next predecessor lies inside that unchanged prefix, so each subtraction uses two original values. Retaining index zero provides the initial value needed to reconstruct the original sequence later.

Forward order instead first stores two at index one. The next subtraction uses that modified two and gives seven at index two; the last uses the modified seven and gives three. It produces [3,2,7,3], a different recurrence.

Forward prefix accumulation applied to [3,2,4,1] reconstructs [3,5,9,10], showing the inverse relation under exact arithmetic. A signed-machine implementation needs every subtraction and subsequent reconstruction sum to be representable. The algebraic inverse does not retroactively make an overflowing intermediate defined.
